clue.text: Job’s showing people this game

blocks.note: first meaning: the quality the biblical Job is proverbial for, which he shows people
second meaning: the solitaire card game played alone

explanation.surface: Someone's work is putting a particular game in front of people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Job's' reads as 'job is', a piece of work; it is the biblical Job, whose long-suffering endurance is proverbial. In Britain solitaire is usually called by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Job's virtue is calm endurance of suffering, and the same word names the British one-player card game known elsewhere as solitaire.

clue.text: Fear changes in lead house?

indicators.note: letters that change are altered in their arrangement and come out in a new order
one thing set in another sits inside it, flanked on both sides

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
Pb is the chemical symbol for the metal lead

explanation.surface: Fear changes inside a house built with lead, perhaps about poisoning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' wants to be the verb or the dog's leash; here it is the metal, symbol Pb. The question mark warns that the definition is an example rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A prefabricated building is one type of dwelling, assembled quickly from factory-made sections, hence the question mark showing definition by example.

clue.text: Something for Scrabble player clutching very quiet drink

indicators.note: to clutch is to grip tightly, so the outer letters hold the inner ones

blocks.note: Scrabble is played with lettered tiles
pp, pianissimo, is the musical marking for very quiet

explanation.surface: A Scrabble player sits quietly nursing a drink during the game.
explanation.walkthrough: Pianissimo, written pp, is the musical direction for very soft playing; p alone is piano, quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: A tipple is an informal word for an alcoholic beverage, usually a favourite one taken habitually.

clue.text: Lady’s year worked out? Too soon to be sure

indicators.note: something worked out has been processed and rearranged into a new shape

blocks.note: all nine letters, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a woman's year has gone well, and is told it is too soon to judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worked out' looks like a question about how the year went, but it tells you to rearrange the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is said when something has only just begun and it is premature to judge how it will turn out.

clue.text: Racer I invested in got round somehow, that’s groovy?

definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for the thing that has grooves

indicators.note: money invested in a venture is placed inside it, so one group goes within another
done somehow means done in some unstated fashion, so the letters fall into an unspecified order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A racer somehow got round the track, and someone wonders if that's cool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groovy' looks like sixties slang for cool; it is literal, meaning full of grooves. All fourteen letters of the two phrases combined are mixed together.
explanation.definitionFit: Corrugated sheet metal is pressed into parallel ridges and channels, so it is literally covered in grooves.

clue.text: Move fast coming from meeting — all opposed

indicators.note: what comes from a phrase is drawn out of its letters, sitting inside it

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Someone hurries out of a meeting where every vote went against them.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the dash, starting in the last letter of 'meeting' and ending in the first two of 'opposed'.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse's fastest pace gives the verb meaning to run or travel rapidly, used of people too.

clue.text: Byword of a daughter, mature

blocks.note: taken as written
d is the genealogical abbreviation for daughter
to mature is to grow older

explanation.surface: A proverb is attributed to a grown-up daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mature' looks like an adjective describing the daughter; it is a verb, to grow old.
explanation.definitionFit: A byword can mean a proverb or common saying, which is exactly what an adage is.

clue.text: Scholarly ones featuring in US volume — factoid given regular exposure

indicators.note: only letters at even intervals are exposed to view, the others staying covered

blocks.note: the American spelling of the metric unit of volume
second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Academics appear in an American book that keeps repeating a trivial fact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volume' suggests a book; it is a measure of capacity, spelt the American way, which is why 'US' is there.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin plural names well-read, educated people collectively, the learned class of a society.

clue.text: One sending up standard poet

blocks.note: par is the normal or expected level
an odist is a writer of odes

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a conventional, run-of-the-mill poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' looks like an adjective for the poet but is its own piece, the golfing par.
explanation.definitionFit: To send someone up is British idiom for mocking them through imitation, which is the work of a satirical imitator.

clue.text: In play actor roars “Pint!” — one to make him wait for it?

definitions.text: one to make him wait for it
definitions.note: a playful description of someone who always delays

indicators.note: letters in play are loose and moving about, free to settle in a different order

blocks.note: all fourteen letters of the three words

explanation.surface: In a stage play an actor bellows for a pint and is left waiting by a slow barman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In play' sounds like the theatre setting; it signals rearrangement. The definition is a whimsical picture of the person who keeps putting the order off.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who habitually delays and postpones tasks is exactly the kind of person who keeps others waiting.

clue.text: European parliamentarian associated with mistake disheartened ruler

indicators.note: losing heart means losing the central part, so the middle letter goes

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
a Member of Parliament
a synonym, before its central letter is lost

explanation.surface: A Euro-MP makes a blunder that leaves a sovereign downcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disheartened' reads as sad, describing the ruler; it removes the middle R of the five-letter word for mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: An emperor is a sovereign over an empire, a supreme monarch and so a kind of head of state.

clue.text: Almost arrive at hill’s energy facility

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of it, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: to arrive at a place is to get there; it loses its last letter
a tor is a rocky hill, found especially on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Someone nearly reaches a hilltop power station.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'hill' just joins the pieces. Tor is a West Country word for a rocky hilltop.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuclear reactor is the plant in which fission is controlled to generate power for electricity.

clue.text: Narrow passage in kitchen, not good

indicators.note: 'not' tells you a letter is left out of the word it governs

blocks.note: a ship's or aircraft's kitchen
G is the abbreviation for good, the letter removed

explanation.surface: A cramped corridor in the kitchen is no good at all.
explanation.walkthrough: A galley is the kitchen on a boat or plane; removing its first letter, G for good, leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An alley is a slim lane or walkway between buildings, too tight for traffic.

clue.text: Not yet approved — global body was concerned about the French

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one part goes round another

blocks.note: the United Nations
to care is to be concerned
le is the masculine French for 'the'

explanation.surface: A proposal is still pending because the United Nations worried about the French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning' after 'was concerned', but it puts the French article inside the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Something cleared has been given official permission, so its negative describes a thing still awaiting authorisation.

clue.text: Places to stay, vacant, as rise subject to review

indicators.note: something under review may be reworked, so the letters are revised into a new order

blocks.note: all twelve letters of the three words

explanation.surface: Holiday lodgings stand empty while a price increase is being reconsidered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise' reads as a price increase being reviewed; it is just letters. In Britain these are parks where people stay in towed or static trailers.
explanation.definitionFit: Caravan sites are holiday parks where visitors lodge in mobile homes or trailers, so they are somewhere to lodge.

clue.text: Pole’s church welcomed by new nations

indicators.note: something new is remade, so the letters take a fresh order
a guest welcomed by hosts is taken in among them, so one part enters another

blocks.note: CH is the standard abbreviation for church
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A Polish person's church is embraced by newly independent countries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' with a capital letter suggests a Polish person; it is an upright post. A capital letter at the start of a clue hides nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A stanchion is an upright bar or post used as a support, which is a kind of pole.

clue.text: Four articles about panjandrum ultimately one detested

indicators.note: being about something means surrounding it, so the outer letters go round
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is used

blocks.note: the English articles an, a, the and a
its final letter

explanation.surface: Four newspaper pieces about a pompous bigwig, who is ultimately loathed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests newspaper pieces; they are the grammatical words, definite and indefinite. A panjandrum is a self-important official.
explanation.definitionFit: Anathema denotes a thing or person intensely loathed, as in 'he is anathema to me'.

clue.text: Imperil objective: wrath follows

indicators.note: coming after places the second part behind the first in the line

blocks.note: an end is an aim or goal
a synonym for rage

explanation.surface: Putting a goal at risk is followed by fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Objective' could be an adjective meaning impartial; it is a noun here, a goal.
explanation.definitionFit: To imperil is to put something in jeopardy or at risk, an exact verbal synonym.

clue.text: After day in Rome, despatched — finally regularly ignored as unimportant

indicators.note: after sets one part behind another in sequence
letters ignored at a regular interval are skipped every other time, leaving the rest

blocks.note: the nones were a fixed day in each month of the Roman calendar
despatched means sent off
second, fourth and sixth letters, the others ignored

explanation.surface: After a day in Rome, something sent off is ultimately dismissed as trivial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' looks like an adverb meaning at last; it is the source word from which alternate letters are kept. The Roman calendar named the 5th or 7th of each month the nones.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not essential can be done without, so it is of little consequence or significance.

clue.text: Cardinal at first toying with experimental liturgy, very ephemeral

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of each word that follows

blocks.clueFragment: toying with experimental liturgy, very ephemeral
blocks.note: the initial letters of the six words

explanation.surface: A cardinal of the church dabbles with a new-fangled, short-lived form of service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal' paints a churchman to suit the liturgy; it means a cardinal number, as opposed to an ordinal like twelfth.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardinal numbers are the counting numbers one, two, three and so on, so any of them fits.

clue.text: Speaker from floor, a Tory

indicators.note: taken from a phrase means lifted directly out of its run of letters

blocks.note: the end of the first word, the whole second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A Conservative member speaks up from the floor of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tory speaking 'from the floor' is the parliamentary picture; the letters run continuously across the three words.
explanation.definitionFit: An orator is a public speaker, especially an eloquent or skilled one addressing an audience.

clue.text: Specialist actor was furious after time, I advised nervously at first

indicators.note: after places one part behind another in sequence
at first points to the opening letter of each word it governs

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to rage is to be furious
taken as written
the opening letters of the two words

explanation.surface: An actor flew into a rage after a while, and someone nervously gave advice at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces read in clue order except time, which 'after' puts in front of the rage.
explanation.definitionFit: A tragedian is a performer who specialises in serious dramatic roles, the opposite of a comedian.

clue.text: Odds? Yes (strange as it may seem!)

definitions.text: Odds? Yes (strange as it may seem!)

blocks.note: surface reading: odd numbers, the opposite of their even partners
setter's reading: betting odds, where one quoted price is named after the opposite of odd

explanation.walkthrough: The paradox is that something odd can be named by its opposite: a betting price of one to one is called by the word for numbers divisible by two.
explanation.definitionFit: Bookmakers quote one-to-one, even money, odds under a name that sounds like the opposite of odd numbers.

clue.text: Quail, caught by old, wide, English river

indicators.note: by means next to, so the parts are set side by side

blocks.note: c for caught, the cricket scoring abbreviation
O is a common abbreviation for old
w, a wide, in cricket scoring
E for English
R for river

explanation.surface: A game bird is netted beside an ancient, broad English river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quail' looks like the bird; it is the verb, to shrink back in fear. Caught and wide are cricket scorebook abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: To quail is to shrink back in fear, just as to cower is to crouch in terror.

clue.text: At outset extremely loud grumbling rattles employee, company painter

indicators.note: the outset is the start, so each word contributes its opening letter

blocks.note: the initial letters of the five words
Co is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A worker is unsettled by very noisy complaining from the start, in a company of decorators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Painter' sounds like a decorator at the firm; it is the artist. El Greco, 'the Greek', was the Cretan-born painter who worked in Toledo, Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Doménikos Theotokópoulos, known by this Spanish nickname, was a celebrated Renaissance artist famous for elongated figures.

clue.text: Group member’s outing authorised

blocks.note: a trip is an excursion
let means allowed or permitted

explanation.surface: A band member's day out has been approved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Group member' suggests a pop band; the group is a set of three, either siblings born together or three notes played in the time of two.
explanation.definitionFit: A triplet is one of three born at a single birth, or one item in any set of three.

clue.text: Again a fight initially about quiet

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so just the opening letter is used

blocks.note: taken as written
its opening letter
re means concerning, as in a letter heading
sh is the call for silence

explanation.surface: Once more a scrap starts up over a demand for silence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is not a container signal here but the word re, meaning concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: To start afresh is to begin anew, once more from the beginning, so the adverb matches.

clue.text: Magnificence of Greece with continent following (not half!)

indicators.note: following puts the next part behind what came before
not half keeps only part, so the second half of the letters goes

blocks.note: GR is the international vehicle code for Greece
and means together with
the continent, cut to its first three letters

explanation.surface: The splendour of Greece, with Europe close behind — 'not half!' being British slang for very much so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'absolutely'; here it is literal, halving the continent's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Grandeur is splendour and impressiveness of appearance or style, matching magnificence closely.
